title: Chapter 21. Of the Liberty of Subjects
paragraphs: Liberty, or FREEDOM, properly signifies the absence of opposition — by which I mean external impediments to motion — and may be applied no less to irrational and inanimate things than to rational ones. For whatever is so tied, or hemmed in, that it cannot move except within a certain space, that space being determined by the opposition of some external body, we say it has no liberty to go further. So of all living creatures, while they are imprisoned or restrained with walls or chains; and of water, while it is held in by banks or vessels which otherwise would spread it into a larger space, we say they are not at liberty to move in the way they would without those external obstacles. But when the impediment to motion is in the constitution of the thing itself, we do not say it lacks liberty, but the power to move — as when a stone lies still, or a man is bound to his bed by sickness.

And according to this proper and generally received meaning of the word, a FREE-MAN is 'he who, in the things he is able by his strength and wit to do, is not hindered from doing what he has a will to do.' But when the words 'free' and 'liberty' are applied to anything but bodies, they are misused; for what is not subject to motion is not subject to impediment. So when it is said (for example) 'the way is free,' no liberty of the way is meant, but of those who walk in it without being stopped. When we say a gift is free, no liberty of the gift is meant but of the giver, who was not bound by any law or covenant to give it. So when we speak freely, it is not the liberty of voice or pronunciation, but of the man, whom no law has obliged to speak otherwise than he did. Finally, from the phrase 'free will' no liberty can be inferred to the will, desire, or inclination, but only to the man — which consists in this, that he finds no obstacle in doing what he has the will, the desire, or the inclination to do.

Fear and liberty are consistent. When a man throws his goods into the sea for fear that the ship may sink, he nevertheless does it very willingly, and may refuse to do it if he wishes; it is therefore the action of someone who was free. Likewise, a man sometimes pays his debt only for fear of imprisonment — and since no one was hindering him from keeping it back, it was the action of a man at liberty. In general, all actions which men do in commonwealths for fear of the law are actions the doers had the liberty to omit.

Liberty and necessity are consistent. As in water, which has not only the liberty but also the necessity of running down the channel, so also in the actions men voluntarily do: those actions, because they proceed from their will, proceed from liberty; and yet, because every act of a man's will, and every desire and inclination, proceeds from some cause — and those causes, in a continual chain (whose first link is in the hand of God, the first of all causes), proceed from necessity. So to one who could see the connection of those causes, the necessity of all men's voluntary actions would appear plain. And so God, who sees and disposes all things, sees also that man's liberty in doing what he wills is accompanied by the necessity of doing what God wills, and no more and no less. For though men may do many things which God does not command, and of which he is not therefore the author, they can have no passion or appetite for anything of which God's will is not the cause. And if his will did not secure the necessity of man's will, and consequently of everything that depends on man's will, the liberty of men would be a contradiction and an impediment to the omnipotence and the liberty of God. And so much (as far as the matter at hand) for that natural liberty, which alone is properly called liberty.

But as men, in order to attain peace and so to preserve themselves, have made an artificial man (which we call a commonwealth), so they have also made artificial chains, called civil laws, which they themselves, by mutual covenants, have fastened at one end to the lips of that man, or assembly, to whom they have given the sovereign power, and at the other end to their own ears. These bonds, weak in themselves, may nevertheless be made to hold by the danger, even where not by the difficulty, of breaking them.

It is only in relation to these bonds that I am now to speak of the liberty of subjects. Since there is no commonwealth in the world that can regulate every action and every word of men (that being impossible), it follows necessarily that in all kinds of action which the laws have passed over, men have the liberty of doing what their own reason shall suggest as most profitable to themselves. For if we take liberty in its proper sense — bodily liberty, that is, freedom from chains and prison — it would be very absurd for men to clamour, as they do, for a liberty they so plainly already enjoy. Again, if we take liberty as exemption from the laws, it is no less absurd for men to demand, as they do, a liberty by which all other men might be masters of their lives. And yet, absurd as it is, this is what they demand — not knowing that the laws have no power to protect them without a sword in the hands of a man, or men, to cause those laws to be executed. The liberty of a subject lies therefore only in those things which, in regulating their actions, the sovereign has passed over — such as the liberty to buy and sell, and otherwise to contract with one another, to choose their own dwelling, their own diet, their own trade of life, and to bring up their children as they themselves think fit, and the like.

Nevertheless, we are not to understand that by such liberty the sovereign power of life and death is either abolished or limited. For it has already been shown that nothing the sovereign representative does to a subject, on any pretext, can properly be called injustice or injury, because every subject is the author of every act the sovereign does — so that the sovereign never wants right to anything, except insofar as he himself is the subject of God, and is bound by that to observe the laws of nature. And so it may, and often does, happen in commonwealths that a subject may be put to death by the command of the sovereign power, and yet neither party do the other a wrong — as when Jephthah caused his daughter to be sacrificed. In that and similar cases, the one so dying had liberty to do the action for which he is nevertheless, without injury, put to death. The same holds when a sovereign prince puts to death an innocent subject. For though the action is against the law of nature, being contrary to equity (as was David's killing of Uriah), yet it was not an injury to Uriah; it was an injury to God. Not to Uriah, because the right to do as he pleased had been given to David by Uriah himself; and yet to God, because David was God's subject, and forbidden all iniquity by the law of nature. This distinction David himself, when he repented the act, plainly confirmed, saying, 'To thee only have I sinned.' In the same way the people of Athens, when they banished the most powerful man in their commonwealth for ten years, thought they committed no injustice — and yet they never inquired what crime he had done, but only what hurt he might do. They even commanded the banishment of men they did not know: every citizen brought his oyster-shell to the marketplace with the name written on it of the man he wanted banished, without actually accusing him; and they sometimes banished an Aristides for his reputation for justice, and sometimes a scurrilous jester such as Hyperbolus, to make a joke of it. And yet one cannot say that the sovereign people of Athens lacked the right to banish them, or that any Athenian lacked the liberty to jest or to be just.
The liberty that writers praise is the liberty of sovereigns, not of private men.

The liberty so frequently and so honourably mentioned in the histories and philosophy of the ancient Greeks and Romans, and in the writings and discourse of those who derive all their learning in politics from them, is not the liberty of particular men but the liberty of the commonwealth — which is the same as what every man would have if there were no civil laws and no commonwealth at all. And its effects are also the same. For as among masterless men there is perpetual war of every man against his neighbour — no inheritance to pass on to the son, or to expect from the father, no property of goods or lands, no security, but a full and absolute liberty in every particular man — so in states and commonwealths not dependent on one another, every commonwealth (not every man) has an absolute liberty to do whatever it shall judge (that is, whatever the man or assembly representing it shall judge) most conducive to its benefit. But with that they live in the condition of a perpetual war, on the verge of battle, with their frontiers armed and cannon planted against their neighbours all around. The Athenians and Romans were free — that is, free commonwealths; not that any particular men had the liberty to resist their own representative, but that their representative had the liberty to resist, or to invade, other peoples. The word LIBERTAS is written on the towers of the city of Lucca to this day in great letters; yet no one can infer from that that a private man has more liberty there, or more immunity from the service of the commonwealth, than he has in Constantinople. Whether a commonwealth is monarchical or popular, the freedom is still the same.

But it is easy for men to be deceived by the specious name of liberty, and for lack of judgement to distinguish between things, mistaking that for their private inheritance and birthright which is in fact only the right of the public. And when the same error is reinforced by the authority of men of high reputation for their writings on this subject, it is no wonder that it produces sedition and the overthrow of governments. In these western parts of the world, we are made to receive our opinions about the institution and the rights of commonwealths from Aristotle, Cicero, and other men, Greeks and Romans, who, living under popular states, derived those rights not from the principles of nature but transcribed them into their books out of the practice of their own commonwealths, which were popular — just as the grammarians describe the rules of language out of current practice, or the rules of poetry out of the poems of Homer and Virgil. And because the Athenians were taught (to keep them from wanting to change their government) that they were free men, and that all who lived under monarchy were slaves, Aristotle put it down in his Politics (book 6, chapter 2): 'In democracy, liberty is to be supposed: for it is commonly held that no man is free in any other government.' And as Aristotle, so Cicero and other writers have grounded their civil doctrine on the opinions of the Romans, who were taught to hate monarchy at first by those who, having deposed their sovereign, shared the sovereignty of Rome among themselves, and afterwards by their successors. By reading these Greek and Latin authors, men from childhood have gotten the habit, under a false show of liberty, of favouring tumults and of licentiously controlling the actions of their sovereigns — and then of controlling those controllers, at the cost of so much bloodshed that I think I may truly say that nothing has ever been so dearly bought as these western parts have bought the learning of the Greek and Latin tongues.

To come now to the particulars of the true liberty of a subject — that is, what are the things which, though commanded by the sovereign, a subject may nevertheless without injustice refuse to do — we must consider what rights we give away when we make a commonwealth; or (what is the same thing) what liberty we deny ourselves by owning all the actions, without exception, of the man or assembly we make our sovereign. For in the act of our submission lie both our obligation and our liberty; which must therefore be inferred by arguments taken from that act, since there is no obligation on any man which does not arise from some act of his own — for all men by nature are equally free. And because such arguments must be drawn either from the express words 'I authorise all his actions,' or from the intention of the man who submits himself to the sovereign's power (which intention is to be understood from the end for which he submits), the obligation and liberty of the subject are to be derived either from those words (or others equivalent) or else from the end of the institution of sovereignty — namely, the peace of the subjects among themselves and their defence against a common enemy.
Subjects have liberty to defend their own bodies, even against those who lawfully assault them.

First, then, since sovereignty by institution is by covenant of every one to every one, and sovereignty by acquisition is by covenants of the vanquished to the victor, or of child to parent, it is plain that every subject has liberty in all those things the right to which cannot by covenant be transferred. I have shown before, in chapter 14, that covenants not to defend one's own body are void. Therefore —

If the sovereign commands a man (even one justly condemned) to kill, wound, or maim himself, or not to resist those who assault him, or to abstain from the use of food, air, medicine, or any other thing without which he cannot live, that man still has the liberty to disobey.

If a man is interrogated by the sovereign, or by his authority, about a crime he himself has committed, he is not bound (without assurance of pardon) to confess it; because no man (as I have shown in the same chapter) can by covenant be obliged to accuse himself.

Again, the consent of a subject to sovereign power is contained in these words: 'I authorise, or take upon myself, all his actions.' In these there is no restriction at all of his own former natural liberty. For by allowing the sovereign to kill me, I am not bound to kill myself when he commands. It is one thing to say, 'Kill me, or my neighbour, if you please'; another thing to say, 'I will kill myself, or my neighbour.' It follows therefore that —

No man is bound by the words themselves to kill either himself or any other man; and consequently the obligation a man may sometimes have, on the command of the sovereign, to carry out any dangerous or dishonourable office depends not on the words of our submission, but on the intention — which is to be understood from the end of submission. When, therefore, our refusal to obey frustrates the end for which the sovereignty was ordained, there is no liberty to refuse; otherwise there is.

On this ground, a man who is commanded as a soldier to fight against the enemy, though his sovereign has right enough to punish his refusal with death, may nevertheless in many cases refuse, without injustice — as when he supplies an adequate soldier in his place; in that case he is not deserting the service of the commonwealth. And allowance is to be made for natural timorousness, not only in women (of whom no such dangerous duty is expected), but also in men of feminine courage. When armies fight, there is on one side or on both a running away; yet when they do it not from treachery but from fear, they are reckoned to do it not unjustly but dishonourably. For the same reason, to avoid battle is not injustice but cowardice. But the man who enrols himself as a soldier, or accepts a press-money, gives up the excuse of a timorous nature; and is obliged not only to go into the battle but also not to run from it without his captain's leave. And when the defence of the commonwealth requires at once the help of all who can bear arms, every man is obliged — for otherwise the institution of the commonwealth, which they have not the purpose or the courage to preserve, was in vain.

To resist the sword of the commonwealth in defence of another man, guilty or innocent, no man has liberty; because such liberty takes from the sovereign the means of protecting us, and is therefore destructive of the very essence of government. But if a great many men together have already unjustly resisted the sovereign power, or committed some capital crime for which every one of them expects death, have they not then the liberty to join together and assist and defend one another? Certainly they have; for they merely defend their lives, which the guilty man may do as well as the innocent. There was indeed injustice in the first breach of their duty; but their bearing of arms after the breach, though it be to maintain what they have done, is no new unjust act. And if it is only to defend their persons, it is not unjust at all. But the offer of pardon takes from those to whom it is offered the plea of self-defence, and makes their persistence in assisting or defending the rest unlawful.

As for other liberties, they depend on the silence of the law. Where the sovereign has prescribed no rule, the subject has liberty to do, or forbear, according to his own discretion. So such liberty is in some places greater and in some less; and at some times more, at other times less, according as those who hold the sovereignty shall think most convenient. For example, there was a time in England when a man might enter into his own land (and dispossess any who wrongfully held it) by force; but in later times that liberty of forcible entry was taken away by a statute made by the king in Parliament. And in some places of the world, men have the liberty of many wives; in others, no such liberty is allowed.

If a subject has a controversy with his sovereign — over a debt, or over the right of possession of lands or goods, or over any service required of him, or over any corporal or financial penalty grounded on a prior law — he has the same liberty to sue for his right as if it were against a fellow subject, and before such judges as are appointed by the sovereign. For since the sovereign demands by force of a prior law, and not by virtue of his power as such, he declares thereby that he requires no more than shall appear to be due by that law. The suit therefore is not contrary to the will of the sovereign; and consequently the subject has the liberty to demand the hearing of his cause, and a verdict according to that law. But if the sovereign demands or takes anything on the pretext of his power, no action of law lies in that case: for everything done by him in virtue of his power is done by the authority of every subject, and so anyone who brings an action against the sovereign brings it against himself.

If a monarch or sovereign assembly grants a liberty to all or any of his subjects, and while that grant stands he is disabled from providing for their safety, the grant is void — unless he directly renounces, or transfers, the sovereignty to another. For since he could openly (if it had been his will) have plainly renounced or transferred the sovereignty, and did not, it is to be understood that it was not his will; and that the grant proceeded from ignorance of the conflict between such a liberty and the sovereign power. So the sovereignty is still retained — and consequently all those powers which are necessary for exercising it, such as the power of war and peace, of judicature, of appointing officers and counsellors, of levying money, and the rest named in the eighteenth chapter.

The obligation of subjects to the sovereign is understood to last as long, and no longer, than the power lasts by which he is able to protect them. For the right men have by nature to protect themselves, when no one else can protect them, can by no covenant be relinquished. The sovereignty is the soul of the commonwealth; once it has departed from the body, the members no longer receive their motion from it. The end of obedience is protection; and wherever a man sees that protection — either in his own sword or in another's — nature applies his obedience to it, and his endeavour to maintain it. And though sovereignty, in the intention of those who make it, is immortal, in its own nature it is not only subject to violent death by foreign war, but also, through the ignorance and passions of men, carries in it, from its very institution, many seeds of a natural mortality, by internal discord.

If a subject is taken prisoner in war, or his person or his means of life are within the guards of the enemy, and his life and bodily liberty are given him on condition of becoming subject to the victor, he has the liberty to accept the condition; and having accepted it, he is the subject of the man who took him, because he had no other way to preserve himself. The case is the same if he is detained on the same terms in a foreign country. But if a man is held in prison or in bonds, or is not trusted with the liberty of his body, he cannot be understood to be bound by covenant to subjection, and may therefore, if he can, make his escape by any means whatsoever.

If a monarch relinquishes the sovereignty, both for himself and for his heirs, his subjects return to the absolute liberty of nature; because, though nature may declare who his sons are, and who are the nearest of his kin, who shall be his heir depends (as was said in the previous chapter) on his own will. If therefore he chooses to have no heir, there is no sovereignty, and no subjection. The case is the same if he dies without known kindred, and without declaration of his heir; for then no heir can be known, and consequently no subjection is due.

If the sovereign banishes his subject, during the banishment that man is not subject. But the man sent on an errand, or given leave to travel, is still subject — though by contract between sovereigns, not by virtue of the covenant of subjection. For whoever enters another's dominion is subject to all the laws of it, unless he has a privilege through the amity of the sovereigns, or by special licence.

If a monarch subdued by war makes himself subject to the victor, his subjects are freed from their former obligation and become obliged to the victor. But if he is held prisoner, or has not the liberty of his own body, he is not understood to have given away the right of sovereignty; and his subjects are therefore obliged to obey the magistrates already in place, who govern not in their own name but in his. For, his right remaining, the question is only one of administration — that is, of the magistrates and officers; and if he has no means to name them, he is presumed to approve those he himself formerly appointed.
